retrievedReferences.summary:
The Experimental Design Assistant (EDA) workflow.
The workflow is not fixed and different users might prefer to do some steps in a different order. A potential workflow using the different functionalities of the EDA is described as follows: (1) The user starts by drawing a diagram (with nodes and links) representing the experiment they are planning. Assistance is provided in the form of examples, templates, and video tutorials. (2) Information is added into the node properties, providing more details about the specific step of the process represented by each node. (3) The “Critique” functionality (see Table 2) enables the researcher to obtain feedback on the diagram and the design it represents. The feedback might prompt a change in their plans or the addition of missing information. This is an iterative process and the user might go through the first 3 steps a number of times. (4) Once feedback from the critique has been addressed and the user is satisfied with the final design, the analysis method suggested by the system can be reviewed (see Table 2). (5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. (10) The diagram can be updated after data collection to enable the user to keep an accurate record (e.g., to record the number of animals analysed if some failed to complete the experiment or if data are missing for other reasons).

A potential workflow using the different functionalities of the EDA is described as follows: (1) The user starts by drawing a diagram (with nodes and links) representing the experiment they are planning. Assistance is provided in the form of examples, templates, and video tutorials. (2) Information is added into the node properties, providing more details about the specific step of the process represented by each node. (3) The “Critique” functionality (see Table 2) enables the researcher to obtain feedback on the diagram and the design it represents. The feedback might prompt a change in their plans or the addition of missing information. This is an iterative process and the user might go through the first 3 steps a number of times. (4) Once feedback from the critique has been addressed and the user is satisfied with the final design, the analysis method suggested by the system can be reviewed (see Table 2). (5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. (10) The diagram can be updated after data collection to enable the user to keep an accurate record (e.g., to record the number of animals analysed if some failed to complete the experiment or if data are missing for other reasons).

stages.text:
### Advisory Plan: Synthetic Sample Process Flowchart

**1. Diagram Structure & Nodes**
The diagram is a linear workflow with a single binary decision point. It contains 7 distinct nodes and 7 connecting edges. All text is in English as requested.

*   **Start Node:** Label "Start". Shape: Rounded rectangle (high corner radius).
*   **Process Node 1:** Label "Receive sample". Shape: Rounded rectangle.
*   **Decision Node:** Label "Quality check". Shape: Diamond.
    *   *Note:* This node splits the flow into two mutually exclusive branches.
*   **Process Node 2 (Yes Branch):** Label "Normalize". Shape: Rounded rectangle.
*   **Process Node 3 (No Branch):** Label "Reject sample". Shape: Rounded rectangle.
*   **Process Node 4 (Yes Branch):** Label "Output". Shape: Rounded rectangle.
*   **End Node 1 (Yes Branch Terminus):** Label "End". Shape: Rounded rectangle (high corner radius).
*   **End Node 2 (No Branch Terminus):** Label "End". Shape: Rounded rectangle (high corner radius).

**2. Relationships & Connectivity**
*   **Start** $\rightarrow$ **Receive sample**
*   **Receive sample** $\rightarrow$ **Quality check**
*   **Quality check** $\xrightarrow{\text{yes}}$ **Normalize**
*   **Quality check** $\xrightarrow{\text{no}}$ **Reject sample**
*   **Normalize** $\rightarrow$ **Output**
*   **Output** $\rightarrow$ **End** (Top/Right terminus)
*   **Reject sample** $\rightarrow$ **End** (Bottom/Side terminus)

**3. Layout Strategy**
*   **Orientation:** Top-to-Bottom (Vertical) flow is selected to clearly separate the "Yes" (pass) and "No" (fail) outcomes without horizontal crowding.
*   **Branching:**
    *   The **"yes"** branch continues vertically downward from the diamond (Quality check $\rightarrow$ Normalize $\rightarrow$ Output $\rightarrow$ End).
    *   The **"no"** branch exits horizontally or diagonally to the side from the diamond, leading to "Reject sample", which then terminates at its own "End" node aligned below or beside the rejection step.
*   **Alignment:** "Start", "Receive sample", "Quality check", "Normalize", "Output", and the primary "End" form a central vertical axis. "Reject sample" and its "End" are offset to the right (or left) to indicate deviation from the main process.

**4. Styling & Constraints Compliance**
*   **Palette:** Fixed renderer palette applied.
    *   Process/Start/End Fill: `#e5efeb` (Light Green-Grey).
    *   Decision Fill: `#f5ead6` (Light Beige/Orange).
    *   Stroke/Arrow: `#355c53` (Dark Teal).
    *   Text: `#203d37` (Dark Teal).
*   **Typography:** Noto Sans Regular. Minimum 14px font size ensured for 1K resolution.
*   **Shapes:** Strict adherence to contract—Diamonds for decisions, Rounded Rectangles for operations/terminators. No icons or images from the reference paper are used.
*   **Content Safety:** No numeric values, statistical claims, or scientific data from the reference image (EDA workflow) are transferred. Only the structural logic of a flowchart is borrowed.

**5. Verification Checklist**
*   [x] "Start" and "End" nodes present and distinct.
*   [x] "Quality check" is a diamond.
*   [x] "yes" and "no" labels explicitly placed on branching arrows.
*   [x] "Reject sample" path terminates independently.
*   [x] "Normalize" $\rightarrow$ "Output" sequence preserved.
*   [x] No reference data (animals, randomization, etc.) included.

(5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. A potential workflow using the different functionalities of the EDA is described as follows: (1) The user starts by drawing a diagram (with nodes and links) representing the experiment they are planning. Assistance is provided in the form of examples, templates, and video tutorials. (2) Information is added into the node properties, providing more details about the specific step of the process represented by each node. (3) The “Critique” functionality (see Table 2) enables the researcher to obtain feedback on the diagram and the design it represents. The feedback might prompt a change in their plans or the addition of missing information. This is an iterative process and the user might go through the first 3 steps a number of times. (4) Once feedback from the critique has been addressed and the user is satisfied with the final design, the analysis method suggested by the system can be reviewed (see Table 2). (5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. (2) Information is added into the node properties, providing more details about the specific step of the process represented by each node. (3) The “Critique” functionality (see Table 2) enables the researcher to obtain feedback on the diagram and the design it represents. The feedback might prompt a change in their plans or the addition of missing information. This is an iterative process and the user might go through the first 3 steps a number of times. (4) Once feedback from the critique has been addressed and the user is satisfied with the final design, the analysis method suggested by the system can be reviewed (see Table 2). (5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out.
